articles.title: Every Band Playing Bumbershoot: Saturday
articles.author: Megan Seling, Rob Moura, Sam Machkovech, Audrey Vann, Julianne Bell, Rachel Stevens, and Charles Mudede
paras: ⭐ 📍 ANTHERS This comparison will only resonate with maybe six people, but I’m gonna say it anyway: If you loved long-defunct Seattle punk rock noise makers pleasureboaters, go see ANTHERS and party like you’re at Healthy Times Fun Club circa 2008. Not a 40-something who lived in Seattle nearly two decades ago? Fine. Here are some more rock bona fides—ANTHERS’ latest singles, “Soup” and “Collector,” were recorded by Ben Verellen of Helms Alee and Joel Cuplin of Constant Lovers. And in 2024, The Stranger ’s contributing concert photographer Brittne Lunniss—who attends hundreds of shows a year—said the band delivered one of her favorite performances, writing, “ANTHERS was the best car crash I’ve ever been in.” Hell yes. ( Upper Courtyard Stage ) MEGAN SELING

📍 Aryana León In a 2024 interview, Aryana León recalls standing in front of the mirror as a young teen, practicing her “lightsaber introduction” as if she were a star on the Disney Channel. Today, she’s flourishing as a pop/R&B artist on the rise, having played her first Capitol Hill Block Party in 2024 and releasing her first EP, PLEASURE , in 2025. Her voice is incredible, warm currents over songs that play like smooth passenger-side car rides by the bay—perfect for a late August day under the shade of the Needle. ( Upper Courtyard Stage ) ROB MOURA

📍 Bexley Lead singer Amanda Hardy is the dark-hair-in-her-eyes girl at your high school who exclusively wore baggy Alice in Chains and Soundgarden T-shirts. Her band Bexley keeps that spirit alive by fusing overdriven, heavy riffs, soulful wails over guitar solos, and a Zeppelin/Sabbath foundation of ’70s rock. Your dad will tap his toes, and you might bang your head. We hope to hear “Female Hysteria” in Bexley’s Bumbershoot set, as its core, Nirvana-like riff evolves into a Kim Thayil–worthy guitar upswell. ( Upper Courtyard Stage ) SAM MACHKOVECH

⭐ 📍 Bikini Kill When Bikini Kill embarked on their first reunion tour in 2019, I traveled to Los Angeles to see it, fearing it’d be a one-time thing. (They’ve since performed approximately 10 million times in cities way closer to me, but I’m not bitter about it, I swear.) See, the Olympia feminist punk band is the reason I went to Evergreen State College; the reason I wasn’t afraid to stand up to know-it-all dudes at said college; the reason I ironed the words “kill me” on a Forever 21 dress in high school. Despite my riot grrl phase blossoming in the 2010s, lyrics to their early ’90s songs like “There are no boundaries on what I can feel” (“Feels Blind”) and “Don’t need you to tell us we’re good / Don’t need you to say we suck / Don’t need your protection / Don’t need your dick to fuck” (“Don’t Need You”) were still just as fresh, jolting, and resonant as they were two (and now three) decades before. ( Mural Stage ) AUDREY VANN

⭐ Blood Orange It’s been 10 years since Dev Hynes, aka Blood Orange, dropped his iconic album Freetown Sound , and I, for one, have never been the same. The lush, dreamy ’80s R&B- and funk-influenced songs soundtracked a sun-soaked summer in my 20s and seeped into my memories. Hynes has collaborated with artists as diverse as Britney Spears, Solange Knowles, Tinashe, Carly Rae Jepsen, Debbie Harry, Sky Ferreira, and Mariah Carey. His last album, Essex Honey , is a meditation on grief and his upbringing in Essex, as well as how music has bolstered him throughout his life. I just know that his Bumbershoot set is going to heal me. ( Fisher Stage ) JULIANNE BELL

⭐ Cain Culto Are you ready to party your ass off? Because no one can do it like a gay icon who used to be an evangelical worship pastor. Born Andrew Padilla, this alt-artist started going by “Cain” as a reference to two things: (1) Cain in the Bible, the scripture’s first recorded bad boy; and (2) the Spanish word for “worship” is “cain,” which hearkens to his Colombian and Nicaraguan heritage. Cain Culto raps, sings, and plays electric violin while dancing like you’re on the floor at your favorite gay bar. While it’s pop music meets Latin rap, there is still an element of worship in Cain Culto’s music. Except now, he’s not asking you to follow Jesus, he’s singing of queer joy and “Uh, fuck Trump, fuck ICE, free Palestine. I’ma say that shit again: free Palestine.” Hallelujah! ( Mural Stage ) RACHEL STEVENS

Chase & Status If Turnstile’s hardcore isn’t your thing, head over to the Mural Stage where London-based DJs Chase & Status (aka Saul Milton and Will Kennard) will close out Saturday night with what’s sure to devolve into a dizzying drum ‘n’ bass dance party. No, they haven’t won a Grammy like Turnstile, but they have won a Brit Award, which is the UK equivalent. Pick your poison. ( Mural Stage ) MEGAN SELING

Die Spitz Die Spitz popped off—first in their home city of Austin, then nationwide—based on their live performances wherein the band’s all-femme roster would trade vocal leads and put out punk so incendiary it would damn near burn the venue down. After winning their local Album of the Year award (someone should start that here!) for their ferocious 2023 EP Teeth , they secured opening slots for bands like Sleater-Kinney and Amyl and the Sniffers. For better and worse, the group has hype coming out of their pores; fans of loud music should strongly consider catching their set. ( Fisher Stage ) ROB MOURA

Joey Valence & Brae Joey Valence & Brae have been collecting Beastie Boys comparisons for years, at least since releasing their 2023 full-length Punk Tactics , and I wanted to hate it, tbh. But their chaotic punk-laced hip-hop tracks that, yes, sound very much like the Beastie Boys and the days when rockstars and rappers collaborated are bursting with sincerity. They sound less like a rip-off and more like a whole-hearted celebration of all the musicians who inspired them to pick up a mic. Hard to be mad at that. ( Fisher Stage ) MEGAN SELING

📍 Juliet Daniel Ever wonder what quitting your tech job at Microsoft to make bedroom pop would sound like? It sounds like Juliet Daniel, because that’s what this hero did. Daniel’s boppable music was born and bred in Seattle, and it sounds like taking the leaps we all want to make but probably aren’t confident enough to take. This sentiment shines brightest while flooded with 2000s nostalgia in the singer-songwriter’s song “Stare You Down.” The parting lyrics would be everywhere on AIM away messages, if only we were all still doing that: If you don’t {want me} ~*~*~I think you’re crazy~*~*~ ( Upper Courtyard Stage ) RACHEL STEVENS

⭐ Lucy Dacus Out of the three boygeniuses, I’ve always had an affinity for Lucy Dacus. With her introspective, storytelling lyrics and her impressive Goodreads profile, she’s truly a writer’s musician. I love the depictions of nascent queerness in songs like “Kissing Lessons” and “Christine,” the crackling slow burn of “Night Shift,” and the righteous fury of “Thumbs.” Her 2025 album, Forever Is a Feeling , finds the singer-songwriter in her hopeless romantic era, with swoony, intimate ballads like “Best Guess” and “Ankles.” I attended her Remlinger Farms performance last summer and watched her officiate a wedding ceremony for seven couples during the show, which will be a difficult feat to top—nevertheless, I’m eager to see what she has in store for Bumbershoot. ( Fisher Stage ) JULIANNE BELL

📍 Meat Hair If you love local Sub Pop darlings Deep Sea Diver (and who doesn’t?), then definitely don’t miss Meat Hair, an experimental jam band in which members of DSD get real weird. ( Upper Courtyard Stage ) MEGAN SELING

Molchat Doma Minsk, the capital of Belarus, is a weird city of contrasts: gold-lined facades on its main streets, and gothic counterculture seeping in its Eastern European shadows. Dark-wave trio Molchat Doma thus sound appropriately Belarusian. Bearded men hunch over synthesizers and guitars—and occasionally a standing, dance-friendly electric drum kit—to bang out shimmering-yet-devilish techno that sprinkles Gregorian chant into New Order’s formula. Don a trench coat and dance darkly, fellow mavens of the night. ( Mural Stage ) SAM MACHKOVECH

⭐ 📍 Oblé Reed Oblé Reed made the most of Seattle’s post-pandemic plate shift, rushing into the city’s devastated hip-hop scene via a tsunami of well-produced, well-written hip-hop titled LINDENAVE! He followed that up with an equally compelling visual EP ( Retrovision ) and a second album on which he broke local containment and brought even more underrated national talent into the fold ( LINE LEADERS ). Today, it’s safe to say that the 24-year-old artist is near the top of the most notable rappers to spawn from our waterlogged loam this decade. Considering he’s one of the few rappers at this year’s Bumbershoot (besides fellow local hero Travis Thompson), you owe it to yourself to see the man work a crowd. ( Upper Courtyard Stage ) ROB MOURA

⭐ Peaches It’s 2026, and we need Peaches’ sexually transgressive electroclash hip-hop more than ever. Luckily, the feminist musician, director, and performance artist returned this year with her first album in over ten years, No Lube So Rude . “When the world is friction, lube isn’t a luxury. It’s a necessity,” Peaches writes. “It’s how you turn that friction into pleasure, into power, into pride.” The icon’s seventh album does just as advertised by acting as a relieving salve for these dry times, slickening the constant thrust of dystopian news with empowering, funny, and celebratory tracks for the dance floor like “Fuck How You Wanna Fuck” and “Not in Your Mouth None of Your Business.” I haven’t seen her on this tour yet, so just take it from Reddit user Senhoegahara, who wrote, “This girl has CRAZY energy. She put on a helluva show. Couldn’t believe she’s almost 60. She was topless the entire show and crowdsurfed for a good 10 whole minutes. Lmfao.” ( Mural Stage ) AUDREY VANN

Pixel Grip If you’ve been looking for a tighter, gayer, and synthier version of Yeah Yeah Yeahs, Chicago trio Pixel Grip would like to slowly sidle up to you at a very sweaty nightclub. Their drums-and-Moog brand of fist-pumping dance-pop might not befit a sunny Seattle Center stage, but their chunky, brzzt-brzzt Moog-synth jams may be worth slapping on your favorite sunglasses and black leather before stomping along to bangers like “Dancing on Your Grave.” ( Fisher Stage ) SAM MACHKOVECH

⭐ 📍 Sera Cahoone *Picture the old lady from Titanic here* It’s been 14 years… since Sera Cahoone has played Bumbershoot! She’s basically writing directly to us with her brand-new album (out August 28, 2026), titled I’ve Missed You All These Years . Girl, we’ve missed you, too! Cahoone’s new music feels like it’s infused with a newfound joy that only comes from the other side of really going through it. Of the new album, Cahoone says, “I want people to feel what I felt and put themselves in the way I felt back then. I want them to think, ‘If she made it through, I can too.’” If you don’t yet know the magic of Sera Cahoone’s blues meets folk meets country, it’s never too late to pull up a chair. If you’ve been a fan for decades, welcome home. ( Upper Courtyard Stage ) RACHEL STEVENS

Silvana Estrada Mexican singer-songwriter Silvana Estrada combines the sparse acoustic guitars and romantic poetry of South American folk revivalist artists Violeta Parra and Mercedes Sosa with the vocal chops of American jazz icons Billie Holiday and Sarah Vaughn. (For fans of Joan Baez, Angel Olsen, and crying at concerts.) ( Mural Stage ) AUDREY VANN

⭐ 📍 Travis Thompson In 2022, the gifted Burien rapper Travis Thompson made a little history by appearing, alongside Marc Maron, on what was then the coolest TV show, Reservation Dogs. Soon after this exposure, Thompson, who is part Navajo, released a music video for his slamming track “Corner Store.” It featured Macklemore, the last superstar rapper to come straight out of this city. Thompson also dropped the NW hip-hop classic “Need You.” Whatever you do, do not sleep on this cat. ( Fisher Stage ) CHARLES MUDEDE

⭐ Turnstile Since their formation in 2010, the Baltimore-based hardcore punk band Turnstile have grown from hometown darling to mainstream breakout success, taking home two Grammys in February and drawing praise from the likes of Hayley Williams and fellow Saturday headliner Dev Hynes of Blood Orange. The group counts Bad Brains and Sade among their influences and mixes hardcore with melodic pop structures to irresistible effect. They’re especially known for their high-octane, mosh-heavy performances, which many fans describe as life-changing. I saw them at WAMU Theater last October, and the sense of joy and community in the room was palpable—I can’t wait to experience it again. ( Fisher Stage ) JULIANNE BELL

XCOMM Teenagers? Playing music!? And it’s good ???? It will never not be hilarious when grown-ass music critics realize that teens can play guitars. XCOMM from Los Angeles are the music industry’s current “omg they’re so young!” obsession. Their blistering skate punk is thrashy, fast, and injected with some nu-metal guitar wailing, and it doesn’t hurt that their debut full-length, Time to Burn , was recorded by Ross Robinson, who’s worked with bands like the Blood Brothers, Korn, and Slipknot. And yes, the drummer is like 14. Get over it. ( Mural Stage ) MEGAN SELING

articles.title: Every Band Playing Bumbershoot: Sunday
articles.author: Megan Seling, Charles Mudede, Rachel Stevens, Rob Moura, Dave Segal, Audrey Vann, and Todd Hamm
paras: 📍 American Flats If you need a break from all the modern music pummeling your eardrums, catch local American Flats, who describe themselves as “a rock and roll band with Americana and punk influences.” It’s not revelatory, it’s not perfect, but it’s a warm hug if you’re longing for those days of seeing Tom Petty at the Gorge every summer. ( Upper Courtyard Stage ) MEGAN SELING

ATARASHII GAKKO! If you love J-pop, synchronized dancing, matching outfits, and songs about burnout culture, you’re gonna love Atarashii Gakko!, a self-described girl group from Tokyo whose antics have amassed more than seven million followers on TikTok. (The highest of any Bumbershoot performer by far.) In 2024, ahead of their Coachella debut, Nylon profiled the group, writing, “Onstage and off, Atarashii Gakko! radiate a chaotic energy, ping-ponging off one another like kids who’ve had way too much sugar…” Sold! ( Fisher Stage ) MEGAN SELING

📍 Daughters of Venus Daughters of Venus, a Seattle-based “alternative rock girl band” (their words), play music that could be the soundtrack for a dramatic reveal during an episode of ABC Family’s hit teen drama Pretty Little Liars . I mean that as a compliment. I fucking loved that show. ( Upper Courtyard Stage ) MEGAN SELING

⭐ De La Soul It’s hard to really capture the wonder De La Soul’s debut album, 3 Feet High and Rising , produced when it dropped in 1989. And the condition of wonder is produced by something that seems to have appeared from nowhere. One other hip-hop album produced, at the time, a similar effect: Public Enemy’s It Takes a Nation of Millions to Hold Us Back (1988). But De La Soul went on to release a string of brilliant albums, such as De La Soul Is Dead and Stakes Is High . Sadly, because one of its members, Trugoy the Dove, returned to the essence in 2023, this show will feature the remaining two, Posdnuos (rapper) and Mason (DJ), of a trio that completely changed the game. ( Fisher Stage ) CHARLES MUDEDE

⭐ 📍 Death Cab for Cutie Death Cab for Cutie? Let’s talk about their tune “Soul Meets Body,” no matter how briefly. Those familiar with the ancient tradition of Western philosophy will not fail, upon hearing this gorgeous indie hit by one of Bellingham’s best, to think of what I rate as Aristotle’s greatest work, On the Soul . The question in that work is precisely the one presented by Death Cab for Cutie. Is the soul identical with the body? Or are they different substances? What is for certain is that my soul is moved by the sensations my body experiences while listening to this tune. ( Fisher Stage ) CHARLES MUDEDE

Goldie Boutilier Smoking cigarettes is bad. But if you’re gonna smoke a cigarette or two, might I suggest listening to Goldie Boutilier? (Not at Bumbershoot, tho—smoking is not allowed, because they care about your health, okay?!) Boutilier’s music hearkens back to a time where you heard new music in a smoky dive bar after your crush dropped coins in the jukebox and pressed a combination of buttons you never thought to put together. Her music is a combination of chill disco, ’70s glam rock, and alt-country. After hearing this music, you find yourself counting the coins jingling at the bottom of the very deep pockets of your high-waisted Wranglers, hoping you have enough to run that newest Goldie Boutilier song back one more time. ( Mural Stage ) RACHEL STEVENS

📍 Hannah Duckworth While music from bands like Evanescence and Flyleaf is having a resurgence, you don’t have to zip open your old CD binder under the passenger car seat to hear this sound, because Hannah Duckworth exists. This Seattle singer-songwriter-rocker has been on the scene since 2023, playing music that makes us remember how much we love pop-punk of yore. From a Duckworth concert, expect everything from acoustic solo guitar strumming to a beginner-friendly mosh pit. Eyeliner and a T-shirt over a long sleeve shirt are not required, but don’t be a loser. ( Upper Courtyard Stage ) RACHEL STEVENS

⭐ 📍 Lucha Luna If you didn’t already know (if not, where have you been??), Latin music has been thriving in the PNW for quite a while. Just cumbia alone has seen a growing list of fantastic acts breaking out in the area, from the Cumbieros to Orquestra Pacifico Tropical. Enter Lucha Luna, the duo of Eva Vasquez (of Toxic Tears) and Thomas Arndt (of Day Soul Exquisite), whose debut EP BRILLA BRILLA announced the act as fully formed—and aimed straight at the jugular. On stage and on record, Vazquez recontextualizes her other band’s punk energy through Arndt’s dense beats, creating a compelling fusion of rhythm and rage. They’re one of the freshest acts on this year’s lineup, and absolutely worth your attention. ( Upper Courtyard Stage ) ROB MOURA

⭐ 📍 Midpak Within Seattle’s robust funk scene, Midpak are the hungry young guns on the rise. The quartet had their big break in 2024 with a phenomenal opening set for Colombia’s Balthvs at Barboza, and more recently they wowed a Hidden Hall crowd while opening for NYC Afrobeat ensemble Antibalas. Without a vocalist, Midpak rely on their extraordinary instrumental prowess to create dynamic tracks that funkify psychedelia—or psychedelicize funk, depending on how you tilt your head. Influenced by early Funkadelic, Santana, and Khruangbin, Midpak have also incorporated elements of house, cumbia, and various African musics. I’ve seen them play 12 times and they never fail to whip folks into a frenzy. ( Upper Courtyard Stage ) DAVE SEGAL

📍 Morgan Paris Lanza There is no question that Seattle is pumping out incredible musicians at an impressive rate. Though Morgan Paris Lanza can regularly be found performing at Barboza, Nuemos, and Fremont’s newer Cosmic Cottage, she fully operates in what she calls the Lanza-verse. In the Lanza-verse, you’ll experience MPL performing a sultry combination of lounge singing and burlesque that sounds like jazz, R&B, and smooth pop. Her music explores love, loss, and transformation through a vintage filter, making you want to send a postcard to an ex-lover: “Greetings from the Lanza-verse! Don’t really wish you were here…” ( Upper Courtyard Stage ) RACHEL STEVENS

⭐ Noname: 10th Anniversary of Telefone You’re trying to tell me that Telefone is already 10 years old!? It feels impossible, probably because 2020–2024 didn’t really happen. I don’t remember it. But it’s true, Noname is celebrating a decade since the release of her debut mixtape, which put the rest of the world on the horn with her and her fellow visionary young artists of Chicago: Saba, Ravyn Lenae, Raury, and Smino. In 2015, she explained that she hoped the album would feel conversational—like being on the phone with someone for the first time—incorporating everything from “the awkwardness to the laughter.” Ten years later, listening to Telefone still feels like catching up with an old friend. ( Mural Stage ) AUDREY VANN

Orville Peck Nobody’s doing it like Orville Peck. (Well, plenty of people in Seattle are doing it like Orville Peck.) The South African–born gay country artist—and former punk musician, although the spirit never quite leaves you—has been selling our American tricks back to us for almost 10 years, albeit with a subversively queer twist. He endeared himself to our city almost immediately upon signing to Sub Pop for his first record, Pony , though he’s since ditched his indie rock roots to go full-on country, earning duets with Willie Nelson, Shania Twain, and other legends of the genre. At this year’s Bumbershoot, expect Peck to run through cuts off his newest equinely titled record, and expect to live, as always, for all of it. ( Fisher Stage ) ROB MOURA

PawPaw Rod PawPaw Rod’s music is medicinal. It cures what ails you. His posi-soul R&B jams—the result of growing up on Maxwell, Prince, the Gap Band, and Bill Withers, he says—will lift you out of a rut and soften your sharp edges. And if there is a God, she will time it so PawPaw Rod plays “Hit ’Em Where it Hurts” during peak golden hour—“Sunshine, bathe me, lately life been crazy.” Preach, PawPaw. ( Fisher Stage ) MEGAN SELING

⭐ Racing Mount Pleasant Racing Mount Pleasant, a seven-piece indie rock orchestra from Ann Arbor, MI, plays sweeping and dramatic songs that scratch the Velvet Teen-shaped hole in my heart. Their songs shift from whisper-quiet to explosions of horns and strings and harmonies while lyrics like “Call it easy, call it quits / Well, that’s not how your story ends,” remind you to keep breathing. Goosebumps. ( Fisher Stage ) MEGAN SELING

⭐ Sextile LA duo Sextile’s music exists at the intersection where agitational post-punk collides with sleazy EBM. Recording for the impeccable Sacred Bones label, guitarist/vocalist Brady Keehn and drummer/vocalist Melissa Scaduto (both handle electronics) are a galvanizing experience live, if the electrifying Freakout Fest show I caught by them at Tractor Tavern in 2023 is indicative. Their newest album, yes, please. , abounds with sweaty and brazen bangers, and given how their songs seem best heard in dank underground clubs full of illicit activities, it may be strange to witness Sextile outdoors in the summer, with children in attendance. But childhood innocence is overrated, right? ( Fisher Stage ) DAVE SEGAL

⭐ Sudan Archives Dropping at random into a Sudan Archives album, you could find yourself surrounded by neck-snapping Low End Theory beats, heart-stuttering tech-house rhythms, glossy Beyoncé-pop, warm sun spots of neo-soul, a sudden splash of dubby reverb, or lush, worldly violin tapestries. At her most captivating moments, the Los Angeles-by-way-of-Cincinnati singer/multi-instrumentalist finds ways to bend many of these elements to her methods at once, which are always punctuated by her sweeping vocals that oscillate between exploratory poeticism and asides that are sassy as hell. ( Mural Stage ) TODD HAMM

⭐ 📍 Suzzallo If you like the Sunny Day Real Estate songs where Jeremy Enigk is especially pissed off, you’re gonna love Suzzallo’s ear-pummeling, guitar-driven rock songs. ( Upper Courtyard Stage ) MEGAN SELING

⭐ 📍 Takuya Nakamura Takuya Nakamura is not your typical electronic-music producer. The trumpeter and keyboardist moved from Japan to the US in 1990 to study at the New England Conservatory of Music under innovative jazz composer George Russell. This was a big fucking deal, as Russell’s concepts influenced John Coltrane and Miles Davis’s modal music. Nakamura applied those ideas to his own playing, doing sessions with Quincy Jones, David Byrne, Lee “Scratch” Perry, the GZA, and many other notables. Check out tracks “BonJah” and “Caged Bird Flying” and the Jon Hassell–esque dub-jazz of Mysteries of the Cosmos for examples of his fascinating fusions. ( Mural Stage ) DAVE SEGAL

TOKiMONSTA Los Angeles producer/DJ Jennifer Lee, aka TOKiMONSTA, has a well-documented sunny side, full of mid-fi disco and funk-inflected vocal house to keep summer festival crowds smiling. Her sets, like her albums, however, also have an impressive range of styles represented, dipping in tempo into ODESZA or Shlomo territory, as well as a thick bag of remix material to grab from. The variety of moods and counterpunches make for blissful ebbs and flows whenever she hits the stage. ( Mural Stage ) TODD HAMM

⭐ 📍 W.I.T.C.H. W.I.T.C.H. are the standard-bearers of Zamrock, a short-lived movement in Zambia ca. 1972–1977 in which young African musicians emulated Anglo-American garage- and psych-rockers to spectacular effect. Unlike most of their Zamrock peers, W.I.T.C.H. have reunited, cut new music, and continued to tour—albeit aided by musicians from Switzerland’s L’Eclair. W.I.T.C.H.’s classic albums bear prime-time Rolling Stones DNA, and vocalist Emmanuel Chanda sang so much like Mick Jagger that he earned the nickname “Jagari.” But later releases such as Zango and Sogolo reveal shocking creative vitality, as evidenced by the songs’ more muscular, funky rhythms and heavier, wilder guitar riffs, while also exhibiting more traditional native styles. ( Mural Stage ) DAVE SEGAL

⭐ Yves Tumor Yves Tumor is many things, but none of those is a shoegazey, progressive Brit-pop outfit, as I initially thought upon discovering their sprawling, psychedelic Safe in the Hands of Love in 2018. To the contrary, YT is the solo project (though rich in collaborators) of Miami product Sean Lee Bowie, who, through a fascinating touch on a multitude of instruments, a globetrotting lifestyle, and a fixation on detailed, texture-forward sound collageing, has found themself at the cutting edge of a genre-straddling sound that both proggy aesthetes and melody-seeking festival wanderers can get lost in. ( Mural Stage ) TODD HAMM

articles.title: Every Arts District at Bumbershoot 2026
articles.author: Megan Seling, Sam Machkovech, Julianne Bell, and Amanda Manitach
paras: ⭐ Bumbermania In which local wrestling crew SOS Wrestling builds a real-deal ring in the middle of the Seattle Center, and dozens of local wrestling superstars (66, to be exact!) fight, tackle, pummel, and toss one another around for a chance at the Bumbermania belt. It’s so fun, so captivating, that I missed part of Janelle Monáe’s headlining set last year because I couldn’t look away. MEGAN SELING

Cat Circus It is my journalistic duty to set the record straight: The cats do not do tricks in Bumbershoot’s Cat Circus. There are no performances. The cats and kittens, all of whom are available for adoption via Motley Zoo Animal Rescue, mostly lounge around on circus-themed kitty decor while people file in for a quick pat or play. Cats are good; Motley Zoo Animal Rescue is great. But lines are long at the Cat Circus that’s not really a circus. You’ve been warned. MEGAN SELING

⭐ Comedy Coop In the past half-decade, Bumbershoot’s Comedy Coop has drawn oversized, wait-in-line crowds, and we get it. Seattle’s stand-up scene has enjoyed a recent, steady rise in quality and quirkiness, thanks to a healthy number of venues and ongoing showcases for locals to work out their boundary-pushing routines. With proven collectives like Pacific North Weirdos (headed by Stranger “Undisputable Geniuses of Comedy” Emmett Montgomery and Derek Sheen), the Disabled List, and #TheBLACKOUT, along with rising showcases like One Man Show (a female/nonbinary showcase) and Laff-a-Ball (nerdy comedy born from Fremont’s popular Add-a-Ball arcade), this year’s comedy options will likely merit their own lengthy queues. Budget your between-bands comedy time accordingly. SAM MACHKOVECH
Euro Bungee Strap into this contraption that looks like something that sprouted out of Doctor Octopus’s back and jump around on a trampoline, if that’s something you’re into! MEGAN SELING

⭐ Fashion Runway Although Seattle is not exactly known for its fashion— The Stranger ’s Charles Mudede called it “the anti-fashion capital of the world” in 2022—Bumbershoot’s Fashion District is a chance for the city’s few sartorial specialists to flaunt their style bona fides on the runway. I’m excited to see New Affection’s “silhouettes that question dominant beauty standards and nod to queer history,” the “small-batch, slow fashion design house” Prairie Underground, Vancouver Indigenous Fashion Week, the teen-run fashion show High Fashion High, and multidisciplinary artist and designer Alter Ego Expressions. JULIANNE BELL

⭐ Flatstock The world’s greatest poster and art show is back! At Flatstock, more than 20 local and visiting independent artists will be displaying and selling their incredible work. Sure, it’s a smaller iteration compared to the early 2000s (when Flatstock would feature hundreds of artists throughout the weekend), but hey, quality over quantity, baby! MEGAN SELING

Free Range Performances Keep a lookout for what Bumbershoot calls Free Range Performances, in which folks like the Rat City Roller Derby skaters and conceptual artist Flatchestedmama pop up around the Seattle Center and do what exactly? And when? Who knows! The mystery is what makes it fun, maybe! MEGAN SELING

Gravity Park You’ll feel like it’s X-Games circa 1997 at Gravity Park, where you can catch skateboard and BMX competitions and demos from Dope Planet, Skate Like a Girl, Ride and Glide, and Alchemy Skateboarding. Also returning this year: 35th North’s Ramp Riot, where the best tricks can win skaters cash prizes! MEGAN SELING

Large-Scale Sculpture & Light Art Come dusk, gather like moths around the candy-color glow of Sparks Designs’ large-scale light installations. The team collaborates with femme and LGBTQIA+ metalworking artists to create monumental shadow- and light-box sculptures inspired by the lushness of our bioregional ecosystems. Presented in more than 30 cities across eight countries, their work may resemble giant paper lanterns or stained glass, but they’re meticulously welded, cast, forged, and cut into intricate forms that cast prismatic patterns across the landscape. AMANDA MANITACH

Magic Dome If you only take one thing away from this printed guide, it should be this advice: Never search for magicians on an algorithmic platform. If you ask Insta, YT, or TikTok if this is your card, they will bombard you with corny street magicians. We took the hit to confirm that Bumbershoot’s new Magic Dome isn’t quite the star-studded selection of modern, likable magicians that we were hoping for, with at least one participating magician calling a child a “drunk midget” in his online magic-trick reel, JFC. But Centralia, WA–based Taylor Kyle is a legit close-up magician, and cheesy as he is, his tricks do blow minds, so there’s that. SAM MACHKOVECH

Merchant Village More than two dozen local vendors—from designers and stylists to jewelers and perfumers—are slinging their goods at the Merchant Village. My money will likely end up in the hands of Delusion Bird Vintage (founded by La Fonda!), Seattle Chainstitch Massacre (peep their Widow’s Bay collection), and Embellish the Truth, where fiber artist Sarah Bolden upcycles old clothes into wearable art covered in beads and sequins and crystals to create ready-to-wear pieces that could carry a modern remake of Desperately Seeking Susan . MEGAN SELING

⭐ PROTEST!: A Visual History of Civil Disobedience in Seattle Seattle is really good at civil disobedience—it’s kind of our love language. When you’re ready for a sensory break (or just want to feed on a little intellectual meat), get over to Art/Not Terminal (A/NT) Gallery, where you can catch up on our city’s history of resistance. From the Red Scare–era strikes of 1919 to chasing the cops out of CHOP, PROTEST! , presented by HistoryLink, is an exhibition of photography and archival imagery that traces the history of our city throwing a middle finger at corruption and capitalism. A fun fact about A/NT: it started as a guerrilla gallery literally born in a downtown bus stop in 1987. It’s gone on to serve as a community art space—the people’s gallery—for nearly 40 years! AMANDA MANITACH

Puppet Playhouse Did you know comedian Ryan Stiles, aka the tall guy from Whose Line Is It Anyway? , was born in Seattle? It’s true! And in 2004, Stiles, who is quite possibly the world’s most famous improv comedian, founded the Upfront Theatre in Bellingham, WA. And this weekend, it’s Stiles’s Upfront Theatre that’s hosting the Puppet Playhouse, which will present both kid-friendly and 18-plus puppet shows. Another fun fact: Stiles was in Hot Shots! Part Deux , which also featured Martin Sheen, who was in JFK with Kevin Bacon. Just two degrees from Kevin Bacon! That has nothing to do with anything. I just really like the movie Tremors . MEGAN SELING

⭐ Rooftop District If you need a break from the crush below, the rooftop is the place to be: a perch overlooking the Main Stage, a glass of wine in hand, and intimate performances by artists like improvisational saxophonist KO SOLO and my current dance obsession, atm/overdraft. Whatever you do this weekend, do not fucking miss atm/overdraft. The inimitable dance duo—Kit Wyatt and Hannah Simmons—suddenly seem to be everywhere I look (though it is still not nearly enough), often concealed behind unforgettable mesh masks and dressed in a tangle of flesh-toned lingerie and boudoir stockings. Their work blends ballet, burlesque, and butoh into an unbroken slow-motion choreography of climbing, collapsing, and folding into one another. It’s gender-bent decadence, oozing an intoxicating mix of terror, sex, and tenderness. AMANDA MANITACH

Una the Mermaid I am absolutely fascinated by professional mermaids, and Bumbershoot will bring an opportunity to see one work her magic. Hawaiian-born, Portland-based underwater artist Una the Mermaid will swim in a 900-gallon gilded glass aquarium, shimmering tail and all. JULIANNE BELL

VIDEORAMA: Northwest Shorts This year’s Bumbershoot quartet of short-film showcases are curated by longtime local org Seattle Film Society, and they each share a communal, watch-for-the-first-time freshness that we sure miss in the home-streaming era. Without any pre-fest video snippets to review, we can’t guarantee any of their quality, but on a novelty and surprise basis, we vote for the 48 Hour Film Fest, since it requires participating filmmakers to make short films with creative and timing constraints. It’s the film fest equivalent of an improv comedy show: probably better live and with a crowd. SAM MACHKOVECH

articles.title: Who Said It?
articles.author: Megan Seling
paras: While waiting for Death Cab for Cutie to take the Bumbershoot stage on Sunday, September 6, see if you can guess who penned each line of morbid prose—Ben Gibbard or 19th-Century gothic writer Edgar Allan Poe!
1. “Deep into that darkness peering, long I stood there wondering, fearing / Doubting, dreaming dreams no mortal ever dared to dream before.”
2. “Oh, how this penchant is a curse / All the way from the cradle to the hearse / And there are days when I wish you’d just become / An acquaintance or a time-to-time someone.”
3. “Thank Heaven! The crisis / The danger is past / And the lingering illness / Is over at last / And the fever called “Living” / Is conquered at last.”
4. “And we watched the plumes paint the sky gray / As she laughed and danced through the field of graves / There, I knew it would be alright / That everything would be alright.”
5. “I have spoken — I have spoken / They have registered the vow / And though my faith be broken / And though my heart be broken / Behold the golden token / That proves me happy now!”
6. “Something about Satan’s dart / Something about angel wings / Much about a broken heart / All about unhappy things.”

7. “We buried our love in a wintry grave / A lump in the snow was all that remained / Though we stayed by its side as the days turned to weeks / As the ice kept getting thinner with every word that we’d speak.”
8. “And it ain’t easy living above / And I can’t help but keep falling in love with bones and ashes / With bones and ashes.”
9. “And neither the angels in Heaven above / Nor the demons down under the sea / Can ever dissever my soul from the soul / Of the beautiful Annabel Lee.”
10. “As they drowned we could hear them screaming / ‘Oh, what a tragic way to see our final days.’”
11. “No blinding light or tunnels to gates of white / Just our hands clasped so tight, waiting for the hint of a spark.”
12. “I stand amid the roar / Of a surf-tormented shore / And I hold within my hand / Grains of the golden sand / How few! yet how they creep / Through my fingers to the deep.”

Answer key: 1. Edgar Allan Poe, “The Raven” 2. Death Cab for Cutie, “I Built You a Tower (a)” 3. Edgar Allan Poe, “For Annie” 4. Death Cab for Cutie, “Grapevine Fires” 5. Edgar Allan Poe, “Bridal Ballad” 6. Edgar Allan Poe, “The Valley of Unrest” 7. Death Cab for Cutie, “The Ice Is Getting Thinner” 8. Death Cab for Cutie, “Here to Forever” 9. articles.title: Sammamish Poised to Pivot Away from Town Center Growth This Fall
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: Councilmembers in the sleepy Eastside bedroom city that is Sammamish face a crucial decision later this fall, in the wake of council elections that tilted the balance of power away from its previous pro-density direction. The impact of the decision will likely be felt for years to come, as city leaders decide whether to step away from a plan that was intended to finally foster the beleaguered Town Center area into something closer to a real downtown for a city of nearly 70,000.

Incorporated in 1999, Sammamish has been trying to foster some type of center city for its entire (albeit brief) existence. In 2008, after years of debate, the council approved a Town Center plan that capped development at 2,000 housing units, despite capacity for many more across 240 acres.

Very little of that plan, which envisioned separate mixed-use "nodes" far away from the main thoroughfare of 228th Avenue SE, came to fruition. One reason was very meager density limits, with developers like the builders of the Village at Sammamish Town Center (home to Metropolitan Market) consolidating their projects on a portion of a lot in order to be able to build up.

"When the Town Center was originally adopted, it was envisioned in part as a place to put the growth. However, the opposite, you could argue, actually happened, and instead of growth happening in the town center, the growth continued to happen as infill in the neighborhoods in the form of single-family residential subdivisions," Sammamish Community Development Director David Pyle said last month.

A few months before the November election, the Sammamish Council voted 6 to 1 to advance study of a growth alternative for Town Center that would have increased the upper limit on the number of units that could be built from 2,000 – where it has stood for nearly two decades – to 4,000. The move was intended to be a step toward creating development standards that allow a mixed-use neighborhood to take shape, rather than Sammamish's current glide path toward more townhouse development in the so-called city center.

Then the voters weighed in, sweeping two pro-density councilmembers out of office and tilting the balance of power away from the bloc that had voted yes last year. In a campaign season that had focused heavily on the Town Center issue, all three councilmembers who took office in January had opposed the idea of studying 4,000 units in explicit terms, citing issues like traffic, infrastructure costs, and "unchecked development."

Josh Amato, who was selected by the new growth-skeptical majority to be mayor in January, had included a banner at the top of his campaign website that read "Josh is opposed to the 4,000 unit upzone in the Town Center."

Now the city has to decide how to move forward, but doing nothing and fully abandoning the Town Center plan isn't an option. Without some density increases within the city, Sammamish doesn't have enough capacity for households across lower income bands, a directive spelled out in House Bill 1220 , which the state legislature passed in 2021.

Moreover, City leaders are eyeing the new Housing Accountability Act , in which the state's Commerce Department reviews the growth plans in select cities to make sure that they're in compliance, and they don't want to end up on the watch list alongside places like Carnation and Bainbridge Island . Before moving to pass an emergency ordinance to get into compliance, Bainbridge had been flirting with triggering the Builder's Remedy, which would have superseded local zoning to allow much greater height and density when builders include a set amount of affordable housing.

In July, city staff sought direction from the Sammamish Planning Commission, with commissioners expressing a clear interest in an "option 4" that would take planned capacity increases in Town Center and distribute that to the city's other commercial centers, like Klahanie, Pine Lake, and Inglewood.

"The biggest advantage of option four, is if you spread it over six or seven [...] different neighborhood centers or subareas, you distribute the traffic, which has been the major, major opposition of the community, going from 2,000 to 4,000, because the town center basically infrastructure is not there to support even the 2,000," commission vice chair Seyed Safavian said.
Safavian noted that Klahanie, currently home to a QFC grocery store, is well-positioned when it comes to a Sound Transit light rail station in Central Issaquah.

"Klahanie has perfect access, and within 5, 10 minutes... access to the freeway, access to the future transit, and Klahanie has really very good roads, road capacity, intersections, roadway improvement infrastructure, and all that that really helps us a lot as far as accepting more housing units, particularly for affordable housing," Safavian said.

Ultimately, it will be up to the Sammamish Council to decide how to proceed, with some moves this year signaling the new majority's potential direction. A unanimous vote last month removes a policy from the city's Comprehensive Plan that would have pushed the city to pursue a designation as a regional growth center, a move that could have unlocked more infrastructure funding for the city – and likely come with requirements for more density.

Just this week, the council voted 5-2 to overhaul its affordability requirements in low-density residential areas, essentially gutting a fee in-lieu program that was intended to act as something of a check on the city's continued proliferation of large single-family homes. Previously, all new homes over 1,500 square feet were required to pay a fee that would be used to fund affordable housing, but that threshold was raised to 1,750 square feet – with the fee only applying to square footage exceeding that threshold.
But the looming Town Center vote will likely be the most pivotal of the year, determining how Sammamish grows for at least a decade.

"Trying what we tried from before, we will end up with the same opposition that we faced from before. It's the same community, it's the same people. Let's try something different," planning commissioner Hisham Elkhawad said. "You said it needs more work. I would rather do the more work and succeed at the end of it instead of trying what we tried, and we failed."
Correction: an earlier version of this article incorrectly stated that three councilmembers lost their reelection bid last year, but the number is two: one seat was an open race.

articles.title: Op-Ed: How Pike Place Market Can Thrive in the Winter Without Car Traffic
articles.author: Gordon Padelford
paras: Seattleites love Pike Place Market, but hate random vehicle traffic pushing through the heart of it. That has been clear over and over again in surveys and polls, so it has come as a shock that the City is proposing to allow all car traffic Monday to Thursday from October through March .

The latest survey from the Seattle Department of Transportation (SDOT), conducted this past June, heard from 5,403 people and found “98% Support: Near-universal community backing for vehicle barriers.” Importantly, the survey also heard “96% Business Agreement: High alignment among local merchants and staff” among 224 respondents.

Limiting general car traffic in the Market is as close to complete political consensus as Seattle is going to get on anything. Support spans the spectrum of Seattle politics from The Stranger and Mayor Wilson, to the Seattle Times and former Mayor Bruce Harrell.
And let’s be clear about what we’re talking about when we say “limiting general-purpose car traffic” or “pedestrianization.”

No one is seriously proposing preventing businesses from loading and unloading (regardless of whether businesses are using personal or commercial vehicles to do so), deliveries from reaching the Market, or emergency vehicles from responding when needed.

We’re talking about restricting unnecessary vehicle trips: tour buses, Ubers, lost tourists rubbernecking in rentals, and visitors who want to drive and park on the street for their personal convenience.
Limiting this unnecessary traffic makes Pike Place more functional, and makes room for what makes Pike Place special.

During the pilot, the Market has continued to function as both a loading dock and a front porch — a place where farmers can vend in the street, musicians can busk, visitors can sit and gather, and businesses can receive the deliveries they need to operate.
The good news is that, overall, the pilot has been successful :

But unfortunately there were never any agreed on success metrics for the pilot, so the debate about it seems to be endless and anecdotal. The latest news is a proposal to scale back the pilot to allow more vehicles on the street Monday through Thursday starting this fall through the early spring — why?

The issue seems to be that a subset of businesses say some of their driving customers are buying less because they find it inconvenient or expensive to park in the attached 800-stall public car parking garage ( Urban Freight Lab memo ). Exactly how many discouraged driving customers we are talking about is not clear. The Urban Freight Lab study found in a survey of 2,546 visitors to the Market that only 14.5% of customers drive (85.5% walk, bike, or take transit), but how many of those feel discouraged by having to park in the garage seems to be unknown — so we’re stuck with anecdotal concerns that seems to be driving this decision (pun intended).
The good news is that there are alternative solutions to retain these picky driving customers instead of opening Pike Place back up to general purpose traffic !

Taking this approach would make for a better shopping experience for the 85.5% of customers who don’t drive, and open up possibilities to grow the customer base even more. Last fall, we interviewed five pedestrianized markets in Cincinnati , Burlington , Boulder , Charlottesville , and London to learn how they stay active and vibrant all winter long. Here are a few possibilities inspired by those conversations:
Pedestrianization would also mean more space for vendors to safely load and unload on the street.
It would mean parents can shop with their children without worrying about random car traffic.
It would mean people with disabilities can walk or roll in the street without worrying about whether they will be seen by a backing-up tourist in a rental SUV.

It would mean that Pike Place is more than a parking lot — it’s both the loading dock and the front porch of the heart of Seattle. It’s a destination for the public to visit, shop, gather, and build community. It’s no wonder 98% of Seattleites want to keep it prioritized for people — the real question is why can’t our governance structures deliver a better Pike Place for everyone?

You can ask them by emailing your thoughts to: Pike Place Market Historical Commission MinhChau.Le@seattle.gov >, Pike Place Market Preservation and Development Authority (PDA) info@pikeplacemarket.org >, SDOT Director angela.brady@seattle.gov >, and Mayor of Seattle mayor.wilson@seattle.gov >.

articles.title: All aboard Amtrak’s sleeker, cleaner new trains
articles.author: Benton Graham
paras: On Charlie Hamilton’s regular Amtrak rides from Seattle to Portland, Oregon, and Vancouver, British Columbia, he passes some of the country’s most spectacular vistas: the Puget Sound coast and the Skagit Valley. On clear days, he can even see Mount Rainier. But perhaps the most beautiful sight is not the natural wonders of the Pacific Northwest. It’s the cars and trucks inching along the highway.

“It’s nice to be able to be going along there and going faster than what people on Interstate 5 are doing. We kind of like that bit,” said Hamilton, who leads the train advocacy organization All Aboard Washington.

Indeed, riding the train in the Pacific Northwest can take about as long as driving. The trip between Seattle and Portland takes about 3 hours and 30 minutes by either mode, even though the train makes six stops along the way.

Amtrak plans to begin rolling out 83 new trainsets, dubbed Airo , this fall, starting with eight on the Pacific Northwest’s Cascades route. The trains will eventually serve more than a dozen routes in places like New England, Pennsylvania, and much of the mid-Atlantic region. The $8-billion investment is expected to reduce trip times on multiple routes, though Amtrak did not say by how much, and the trains can reach speeds of up to 125 mph. The Cascades trains will also carry 317 passengers — significantly more than the current Cascades rolling stock — and will boost reliability and comfort, according to an Amtrak spokesperson.

Improved hardware could also help advance All Aboard Washington’s vision of more frequent rail service in the region. “Having trains once an hour would be very helpful, and the Airo trainsets would make it possible to do that,” Hamilton said.

The Airo trains also represent a significant and long overdue refresh for Amtrak, which still has trains that date to the 1970s. The carrier has said the new hardware will provide “significant environmental benefits” while making the rider experience more pleasant. The rollout follows the introduction of new NextGen Acela trains on the Northeast Corridor last summer.

Amtrak’s refresh comes after the Biden administration made a historic $66 billion investment in passenger and freight rail through the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act. But it arrives at a tumultuous moment. Despite Amtrak setting ridership records for two consecutive years, the Trump administration has proposed severe cuts to passenger rail funding. Still, the federal government did announce $3 billion in funding, including $2 billion to purchase trains, for Amtrak in August.

Rail carries 8 percent of the world’s passengers, yet accounts for just 2 percent of global transportation energy demand. In that sense, the Airo trains will help make a clean form of transport even cleaner.

Alex Scott, a professor of supply chain management at the University of Tennessee-Knoxville, said rail’s efficiency comes in part from carrying many people at once. “If you can get a fully well-utilized rail car, be it humans or products, those are still more efficient than everybody going in different cars, even if they’re electric cars,” he said.

The trains, built in the U.S. by Siemens , feature electric and diesel propulsion, allowing them to operate on both conventional and electrified routes. While much of the U.S. passenger rail network remains unelectrified, employing new diesel-powered trains can still reduce emissions. “The locomotives they make now, even if they’re not electric, are a heck of a lot cleaner than the old ones, and so upgrading equipment, be it electric or not, is a good answer,” Scott said.

Airo locomotives meet the Environmental Protection Agency’s Tier 4 emissions standards — the agency’s strictest rules for locomotive engines — significantly reducing particulate matter and nitrogen oxide emissions.

Riders on the Northeast Regional route will climb aboard Airo trains in 2027. The new rolling stock will especially benefit riders traveling between Virginia and the Northeast who can wait as long as an hour at Union Station in Washington, D.C. while Amtrak swaps the diesel engine it uses south of the capital to the electric one it uses northbound to Boston. The new trains can quickly transition from diesel to electric power without changing locomotives.

“It’s a win for the environment, it’s a win for the people that are sitting in traffic,” Virginia Passenger Rail Authority spokesperson Karina Romero said. “We definitely want more trains in Virginia.”

Virginia has invested $6 billion in its Transforming Rail in Virginia program. According to Romero, the combination of new trains and improved infrastructure will give riders a more reliable experience.
“You can put down fabulous infrastructure and great tracks,” she said, “but you’ve definitely got to have the equipment to roll on.”
This story was originally published by Grist with the headline All aboard Amtrak’s sleeker, cleaner new trains on Aug 19, 2026.

articles.title: UW Tacoma Aspires to Double Enrollment, Become Downtown's Largest Park
articles.author: Carolyn Bick
paras: It wasn’t long into her tenure before Sheila Edwards Lange, the University of Washington-Tacoma’s new chancellor, noticed something puzzling: private companies were buying buildings in what appeared to otherwise be the university’s campus footprint.
“I thought we owned all of that property, and so when I saw new highrises going up, I thought, ‘Well, how is that possible?’” Lange said.

At the time, developers were also advocating for zoning changes in the campus’ footprint. There was no way the campus could grow to realize any of the aspirations laid out in its old campus master plan , she said, “because our old campus master plan also called for us to be 10,000 students once we were fully built out. […] I was very alarmed — not that folks were doing what they do, which is building housing, which we need, but that the future of the campus was really at risk.”

Lange became the university’s chancellor in 2021. In addition to handling university operations and strategy during the early stages of the Covid pandemic, she had also inherited the legacy of a particular kind of expansion strategy the university had employed since it first opened its doors more than 35 years ago. Instead of having a traditional campus, the university has historically bought up empty buildings — many of them leftover from Tacoma’s industrial past — in the surrounding area, and converted them into classrooms. The 22 buildings the campus now owns are spread over 46 acres.

Now, that’s all changing. Complete with new buildings, the university is pursuing a central campus design meant to (literally) center student life and further its stated goal of reaching 10,000 full-time undergraduate and graduate students.

But a design focused on student life doesn’t necessitate siloing the students from the wider community. Instead, the design intentionally keeps specific corridors and sightlines open and introduces significantly more greenspace to foster community connection and connection with nature. It also preserves significant older buildings on campus, alongside creating new ones to expand student living and dining options.

When UW Tacoma opened in 1990, it didn’t have a dedicated campus in the traditional sense. Conceptualized as an option for transfer and graduate students, the university aimed to serve a South Sound population for whom leaving the area, let alone the state, was not an option.

At the time, there were several otherwise empty buildings connected with the city’s past as the western terminus for the Northern Pacific Railroad. The university was originally housed in one building, the historic Perkins building, which the university leased and did not own. The university could only accommodate 187 students and only offered one degree: liberal studies.

But that swiftly changed. In 1997, the university moved office operations to its current, permanent location on Pacific Avenue, and continued to grow and expand, taking up classroom residence in otherwise empty buildings.

The university now serves about 5,000 students and operates in several converted warehouses and historic buildings in the area. Of the university’s 22 buildings, 18 are historic. Roughly half of the university’s students matriculate directly from high school, while the other half enroll later in life. Many utilize the multiple modes of transit readily available to get to the university.

Over the years, as the university bought up empty buildings for university, a distinct campus footprint emerged. That footprint holds several older buildings, including culturally significant gathering places, and even a tree that is more than a century old.

Following Lange’s observation about the private companies buying up buildings within the campus footprint, the university put out a request for proposals. Given that the university could only afford to pay $350,000 for design work, they didn’t think they would get many bidders, Joe Lawless, the university’s chief strategy officer, said — but “we got 18 [bids].”

That the Bjarke Ingels Group (BIG) was one of those bidders came as even more of a shock, Lawless said, after the university chose to partner with the firm. BIG is a 20-year-old, international architecture and design firm that places ecology, natural connection and sustainability at the center of its work. Its team has won dozens of awards for architecture and design, and has held exhibitions around the world.

Yu Inamoto, a BIG associate and one of the campus design team members, said in an email that BIG threw its hat in the ring to design the campus because the firm saw the sheer potential for the area and the campus.

Neither the university nor BIG worked in a vacuum. Lawless said that BIG “did a really good job” of engaging not just students and faculty, but community members in the process. He estimated that about 80 community groups gave feedback on the project.

The design that emerged was one that prioritizes green space and a space for both students and the wider Tacoma community to thrive. The design intentionally places the central commons area next to the new campus dorms, and specifically creates sightlines to the waters of Puget Sound, and to Tahoma, also known as Mount Rainier.

“The day before they published the final version of the plan [… Inamoto] called me and said, ‘I need you to go up to that corner and stand precisely at the corner and take a picture of the mountain because we need to make sure the access is perfectly aligned from that corner to the peak of the mountain,’” Lawless said.
Right now, where the university sits shows up as a bright red splotch on heat maps, Lawless said, but he refers to the future campus as “Tacoma’s largest park.”

After speaking with residents, Lawless realized just how important it is to make the space into a center not just for academia, but for the wider public. Several residents he spoke with were elders, he said, and they told him that the areas around the current campus footprint are where they spend the most time — “your campus is our park. Your campus is where we go to have our trees and open space. […] It's where people are and you feel safer.”
Inamoto said that in designing the UW Tacoma campus master plan, the company wanted to weave public and greenspace together into the university environment.

“By proposing a cascading urban landscape that brings together these open spaces, we can better connect the campus internally while also integrating it more naturally within Tacoma,” he explained. “This way, students can feel more ingrained in both the campus community and the broader neighborhood.”

In addition to the green-centric layout, Inamoto said that BIG suggested the university work with one of Tacoma’s native tree programs, Grit City Trees , and plant trees along sidewalks and open space.

Despite data showing nationwide college enrollment steadily dropping over the last decade and projected to continue that same downward trend, UW Tacoma aims to double student enrollment from 5,000 students to 10,000 students.

New student housing and dining options will play a role in making going to school at UW Tacoma more affordable and attractive for students. The university plans to create both a more traditional residence hall that will have between 400-500 beds and a dining hall. Lange said that the university expects to open the residence hall in 2029.

The university has an apartment building where mostly older students and graduate students live. While that building has two apartments set aside for emergency housing for housing-unstable students, there are no other university living options for students. UW Tacoma also does not have a dining hall.

According to the university’s most recent survey , 55% of UW Tacoma’s students are food insecure, while 36% are housing insecure. These are higher than normal percentages, Lange said, and having the option of a residence hall and a dining hall will help relieve some of this burden.

“Having a traditional residence hall means they don't have to have credit checks in order to get housing,” Lange explained. “They can get nine months or 12 months, if that's what they want, but they don't have to sign a year-long agreement the way they would in a commercial housing development.”

The university hasn’t yet determined the cost to live in the planned residence hall or have a meal plan, but the university’s director of communications, Elizabeth Metcalf, said in an email that the goal is to make living and dining more accessible for students.

“As we develop these offerings, affordability, flexibility and access will remain key priorities,” Metcalf said. “Because food costs can fluctuate and we are still in the early stages of negotiations with a food service provider, meal plan pricing will not be available until closer to the dining hall's anticipated opening in autumn 2029.”

Mentha Hynes-Wilson, vice chancellor of student life, said that centering students is one of the university’s goals in the new campus design, which the university is hoping will entice more students to enroll. Deciding to enroll in a school is not just about academics, she said. It’s also about whether a student can see themselves succeeding, staying, and belonging in a community.

“The residence and dining hall are designed to feel welcoming, connected, and full of energy. Open spaces will flow into more intimate gathering areas, creating opportunities to meet friends, study, collaborate, and build community. Flexible spaces, courtyards, a kitchenette, and quieter areas will support everything from events and music practice to studying and recharging,” Hynes-Wilson said in an email. “We’re also excited to expand living-learning communities, connecting where students live with how they learn. Students can study together, participate in shared activities, build friendships, and develop relationships with peers, faculty, and staff that make residence life an extension of the educational experience.”
“Ultimately,” she continued, “we want prospective students to walk onto this campus and think, ‘This is where I belong. This is where I want to build my future.’”

Lange said that the university hasn’t set a specific date for the 10,000-student enrollment target — she sees it happening over the next 30 years — but there are specific dates that the university plans to complete key buildings. Provided the university gets capital funding from the state, the university will complete renovations of its historic buildings by 2030, and projects that the park portion of the campus will be completed in the autumn of 2031.

Like most United States institutions, the university sits on land whose history is fraught with colonization and racism. Tacoma’s history includes the forced removal of Indigenous people , anti-Chinese riots , the incarceration of Japanese Americans , and the continuing legacy of redlining . It is this history that the university has long worked to address, including in the new campus’ design.
In addition to meeting with city leaders, Lange said, the university has also made a point of regularly meeting with and incorporating feedback from the Puyallup Tribe.

“What we've heard from them is that they really feel like we are listening to them and incorporating everything that they are advising us to do into the plan, like story poles and art and the desire to one day have a longhouse here on campus,” Lange said.

At its northernmost edge along Tacoma Avenue, the university borders on the Hilltop neighborhood. The Hilltop is an historically Black neighborhood that evolved from redlining and racist lending practices. The community has recently faced increased displacement pressure, as Tacoma has become a regionwide destination for people escaping higher rents elsewhere, which has in turn led to rents jumping in Tacoma. Expanded services, such as the Hilltop extension of the Tacoma streetcar , have boosted interest from developers and real estate investors. The combination has driven up property values beyond what many generational residents can afford.
The university said it has made a point of prioritizing the Hilltop community’s concerns, needs, and wants.
“We were very conscious of not wanting to contribute to further gentrification of the Hilltop,” Lange said.

“And one of the things that was most surprising and disturbing for me was that people really felt like […] the campus had really turned its back on the Hilltop in some ways, because that part of our campus is really unkempt. It is overgrown and it just doesn't look very welcoming or inviting.”

articles.title: Fall 2026 Service Change: Pierce County and South King County
articles.author: Michael Smith
paras: Starting August 29, King County Metro, Sound Transit, and Pierce Transit will be making changes to bus routes in south King County and Pierce County. Most of these changes are in response to the Federal Link Link Extension that opened in December 2025. Service changes in east and north King County will be discussed in future articles.

Across this sub-region, the biggest change is Sound Transit’s Route 574. Route 574 will be truncated at Federal Way Downtown station (instead of SeaTac) and will now run every 15 minutes. At the southern end of the route, the stop at Lakewood Transit Center will be replaced by a stop at Lakewood station.

Routes throughout south King and Pierce Counties will be adjusted in a few weeks. See full list of changes below, or skip to Burien and SeaTac , Kent and Des Moines , Auburn and Federal Way , Pierce County , or Night-Owl changes.

Route 121 will be partially restored to provide eight peak hour trips (four AM and four PM) between Burien Transit Center and downtown Seattle. This route will take just 37 minutes compared to 53 minutes on the H Line.

Route 156 will have a slightly revised routing on its trips between Southcenter and Kent Des Moines station. The route will no longer serve the McMicken Heights loop (dashed blue line on the map). The route will also have expanded service, running from 4am to 11pm on weekdays and 4:30am to 11pm on weekends.
DART Route 631 will now have weekend service. The route will operate the same schedule on Saturday and Sunday as it does during the week.

Route 164 is a new route that will replace the southern half of the current Route 165. Route 164 will run every 15 minutes during the day, every day. Some of the route’s northbound trips will continue to Route 166. Route 166 replaces the northern segment of Route 165. Buses will run every 15 minutes during peak hours and every 30 minutes during the rest of the day. Every southbound trip will continue to Route 164.
Route 168 will have a few additional trips added to provide 15 minute frequency during peak hours.
Route 181 will have improved weekday frequency and addition trips that run until midnight.
Route 182 will have earlier and later trips each day and will now be through-routed with Route 187.
Route 183 will add service on Sunday and run earlier and later on weekdays and Saturday.
Route 187 will be adjusted to run on 320th St and Hoyt Rd in both directions. The route will through-run with Route 182.

DART Route 902 is a new route that will replace DART Route 901. Route 902 has a DART service area in Mirror Lake. Every Route 902 trip will continue to/from a Route 903 trip. DART Route 903 offers a southern route via SW Campus Dr back to Federal Way Downtown station. Route 903 will have increased frequency with trips running every 30 minutes.

King County Metro is introducing two new Metro Flex pilot areas in Federal Way and Auburn. The Federal Way area is anchored at Federal Way Downtown station while the Auburn area is set near Auburn station and transit center.

Pierce Transit’s network is relatively stable for this restructure. Route 11 is getting a new northbound trip at 2pm on weekdays and several other trip times have been adjusted to accommodate the new trip. Route 212 will have a new southbound trip on Sundays at 7:08pm. Pierce Transit is also adding a new westbound trip to Route 214 on Sundays at 8:44am. The agency is also adjusting the schedules for an assortment of routes to improve reliability and reduce transfer times. Sound Transit is removing routes 580 and 586 in Pierce County.

South King and Pierce Counties have two big changes in overnight service. The A Line will now run every 30 minutes between midnight and 4am. Sound Transit is replacing Route 570 with Route 597. Route 597 will provide night-owl service every 30 minutes between Lakewood and Seattle, via Tacoma Dome and SeaTac.

articles.title: Pike Place Pedestrian Pilot Poised to Scale Back for Winter
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: In a move that will likely be a tough pill for Seattle urbanists to swallow, the current pedestrian pilot at Pike Place Market is set to get scaled back to three days a week in October, as the Seattle Department of Transportation (SDOT) tries to find an equilibrium that pleases all stakeholders at the Market. SDOT's proposal would only implement "soft closures" of Pike Place between Pike Street and Virginia Street from 11am to 4pm Friday through Sunday, with "hard closures" with full barricades only implemented during special events.

Outside those weekend and event days, at least through March 31, all vehicles would be allowed to use the corridor without restrictions. According to SDOT's proposal, set to be presented to the Pike Place Market Historical Commission next week, new signage will instruct drivers to yield to pedestrians, with many of the barriers added to manage the busy street through the FIFA World Cup removed.

The current pilot program restricts vehicles simply wishing to drive through the street from accessing Pike Place from 10am to 4pm daily, and has been a smashing success by most metrics. Sales data shows increased business and a jump in visitors, especially locals heading to the Market more often. But it hasn't been viewed as a positive change by many inside the Market, including a substantial slice of business owners and Market advocates.

The question of how the pilot would evolve toward a more permanent iteration has remained an open one, with SDOT holding stakeholder meetings throughout the spring and into the summer to come to a consensus. In addition to SDOT staff, those meetings have included the Pike Place Public Development Authority (PDA), the Pike Place Merchants' Association, the Historical Commission, and a representative from Mayor Katie Wilson's office.

Next week's presentation notes that a June survey of nearly 5,500 Market visitors found "near universal" support for vehicle barriers at Pike Place, with only 2% not on board. In the survey, 38% of respondents affirmed the idea that there was an increase in pedestrian safety, and 25% cited a more welcoming environment for Market visitors.

But a presentation slide referencing "key learnings from summer operations" asserts that signage updates could "improve clarity to reduce confusion of who may enter and when." If SDOT surveyed visitors on whether they'd like to see the pilot scaled back for winter, the department has not released those findings.

The shift to weekend-only operations through the winter mirrors a recommendation made by the University of Washington's Urban Freight Lab (UFL), which conducted interviews and surveyed both merchants and visitors over the course of this year. But the information relied on to make that recommendation is anecdotal, and does not appear to be based on any data that suggests the benefits of pedestrianization wouldn't continue to be seen through the winter months.

"This recommendation stems from both the merchant interview/survey and analysis of the visitor survey," the UFL's technical memo based on its analysis, released last month, stated. "Merchants reported reductions in sales or reduced growth was particularly acute during the winter holiday season. The typical 'busy season' occurs between May and September when the maximum number of workers are employed for over 70% of merchants. This corresponds to visitor activity: over 70% of reported visits occur between May and September."
In shifting to a scaled-back schedule for winter, the new plan makes a big concession to the idea that the pedestrian pilot is hurting a subset of businesses within the Market.

"The Merchants report relying on local shoppers heavily during winter months," the memo continues. "Visitors who travel to the Market by car are more likely to visit between October and April than visitors by other modes. Allowing access to passenger vehicles during these months would support Market businesses while minimizing conflicts with pedestrians."

During "full closures," the crash-rated Archer barriers that have been in place this summer would be replaced with more easily movable barricades, suggesting the department has moved beyond an initial safety-related justification for those barriers that was cited in the wake of the 2025 truck attack in New Orleans.

Bollards that had been added to the sidewalk at First Avenue and Pike Street would be removed, with retractable bollards in the street an uncertain prospect given that the ground underneath is not actually solid and features an " areaway " of the type found all around downtown.

Just last week, the nonprofit Allied Arts of Seattle – which holds two seats on the Market Historic Commission – held a discussion on the future of street access on Pike Place, which featured Pike Place Public Development Authority (PDA) Chief Operating Officer Katie Trent and SDOT's Radcliffe Dacanay, who is managing the access project.

"The needs of the market are a little bit different in the fall and winter, so we've been asked to think about what are some of our options, and this would be one of them: Monday through Thursday," Dacanay told attendees. "The conversation is constant, and we want to make sure we're also hearing the voices from the constituency, the merchants' association. So that has been all part of the process, and all of that feedback is coming into SDOT to our engineering department. We're not making decisions off on our own. We're constantly in communication with the PDA, asking what works, what doesn't work, how might we adjust, and it can go from details of the signage. Should we say 11 to 4, 10 to 5? What color? All of these things. We're having that conversation."

As the day-to-day operator of the entire Market, having the PDA's buy-in for the pedestrian pilot's next phase will be pretty essential, with Trent making it fairly clear last week that the PDA is on board with the direction that things are trending in. It was under the leadership of PDA President and CEO Rachel Ligtenberg, who was hired in late 2024, that the pilot was able to happen in the first place.

"There are as many opinions on the street as people providing them. Visitors are generally aligned [...] in generally preferring fewer cars on the street. But we know that grocery merchants and their customers skew much more heavily in favor of access to Pike Place to make their grocery shopping trips happen quickly," Trent said. "I think we're in a really great place coming into our next [iteration] with MHC and the proposal for fall and winter."

The panel was moderated by John Turnbull, the PDA's former Director of Asset Management, who provided a defense of allowing vehicle access along the street that echoed previous odes to the prior status quo, like former city councilmember Peter Steinbrueck calling the mixing of traffic modes "zesty" in 2022 . Turnbull now serves on the Honorary Advisory Board for Friends of the Market, a group that has recently been trying to throw cold water on the positive sales data coming out of the Market.
"What I think is lost by any kind of strict regulation of what happens on the street is a sense of theater and surprise and mystery," Turnbull said.
Gordon Padelford, Executive Director of the Seattle Street Alliance, offered a defense of the current iteration of the pilot that SDOT seems poised to shift away from.

"We've got a number of opinions on what constitutes like a delicate ballet. I don't think random cars driving through the middle are part of that ballet. I think they are a hindrance to people's shopping experience," Padelford said. "I think that's why we've heard in some of the feedback that there's real frustration around what does the signage mean, because a lot of visitors are hoping to have that experience being able to walk with their families down the street, being able to push a stroller, push a wheelchair down the street, and not deal with the random vehicles. So I would say, if you're not actively loading and unloading, it's really not a good use of the street."

The Market Historical Commission will be asked to sign onto the pilot's next iteration at its August 26 meeting, with the certificate of approval for the current phase expiring at the end of September.
An earlier version of this story incorrectly attributed a quote from John Turnbull to Ben Frey of Don & Joe's Meats. We regret the error.
Doug Trumm contributed reporting to this story.

The list includes basic burgers done brilliantly, but also offers exceptions for variations that are, well, exceptional. Some of these restaurants are easily recognizable as hamburger havens, while others come from places ranging from an ice cream shop to a dive bar to a Guamanian restaurant . No matter what, these stops all have one thing in common: a damn tasty burger.
For the latest update, in June 2026, we added Burgers by Ming, De La Soil, and Ken’s Market.

A $ means entrees are mostly under $10, a $$ means entrees are mostly under $20, $$$ means under $30, and $$$$ means entrees are more expensive than that, or it is primarily a tasting menu restaurant.
Know of a spot that should be on our radar? Send us a tip by emailing seattle@eater.com . As usual, this list is not ranked; it’s organized geographically.
